questions.question: Let $V$ be a real vector space with inner product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$. Which condition on vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k\in V$ makes them an orthonormal set?
options: $\boldsymbol{q}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{q}_i=1$ for every $i$, with no condition for $i\neq j$

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_n$ be an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (with $n\ge2$), with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$. Which modified list is again an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$?
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with an inner product. Which statement about orthonormal bases of $V$ is correct?
options: Only $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product has one, namely the standard basis
$V$ has one only if some basis of $V$ is orthogonal from the start
$V$ has one, and every orthonormal set in $V$ extends to one
$V$ has one, but extending an orthonormal set may require changing its vectors

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$ be orthonormal vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, and suppose $\sum_ic_i\boldsymbol{q}_i=\boldsymbol{0}$. Which argument shows that every $c_j=0$?
options: Taking the inner product with $\boldsymbol{q}_j$ leaves $c_j=0$
Unit vectors are nonzero, and nonzero vectors are always independent
Vectors pointing in different directions are always independent
An orthonormal set always has exactly $n$ vectors, so it is a basis

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$ be orthonormal vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$. When do they form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: For every $k$, since orthonormal vectors are independent
Only if they are the standard basis vectors, up to order and sign

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, which pair of vectors is orthonormal?

In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, $\boldsymbol{q}_1=\tfrac{1}{5}(3,4)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_2=\tfrac{1}{5}(-4,3)^{\top}$ form an orthonormal basis. What are the coordinates $(y_1,y_2)$ of $\boldsymbol{x}=(5,0)^{\top}$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{x}=y_1\boldsymbol{q}_1+y_2\boldsymbol{q}_2$?

In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, the vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(2,-1,2)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,2,0)^{\top}$ are orthogonal. Which pair is the orthonormal set obtained by normalising them?

Let $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2,\boldsymbol{q}_3$ be an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, and let $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{q}_1-2\boldsymbol{q}_2+2\boldsymbol{q}_3$. What is $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|$?
options: It cannot be found without the entries of the $\boldsymbol{q}_i$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, $\boldsymbol{q}_1=\tfrac{1}{3}(2,1,2)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_2=\tfrac{1}{3}(1,2,-2)^{\top}$ form an orthonormal basis of a plane $W$. What is the orthogonal projection of $\boldsymbol{x}=(0,9,0)^{\top}$ onto $W$?

Let $\boldsymbol{b}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{b}_n$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, and write $\boldsymbol{x}=\sum_ic_i\boldsymbol{b}_i$. For which bases does $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2=\sum_ic_i^2$ hold for every $\boldsymbol{x}$?
options: For every basis of pairwise orthogonal vectors
For every basis of unit vectors

questions.question: Let $Q$ be an $n\times k$ matrix with $k<n$ whose columns $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$ are orthonormal in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$. Which statement about $Q^{\top}Q$ and $QQ^{\top}$ is correct?
options: Neither product is an identity matrix

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, let $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$ ($k<n$) be an orthonormal basis of a subspace $W$, extended to an orthonormal basis $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_n$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. What do $\boldsymbol{q}_{k+1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_n$ form?
options: An orthonormal basis of the set $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus W$
An orthonormal basis of the orthogonal complement $W^{\perp}$
A second orthonormal basis of the subspace $W$
A basis of a complement of $W$ that need not be $W^{\perp}$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, the vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_1=\tfrac{1}{3}(2,1,2)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_2=\tfrac{1}{3}(1,2,-2)^{\top}$ are orthonormal. Which vector $\boldsymbol{q}_3$ completes them to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$?

In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, the basis $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,1)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,-1)^{\top}$ is orthogonal but not orthonormal. What are the coefficients $(c_1,c_2)$ with $(5,1)^{\top}=c_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+c_2\boldsymbol{v}_2$?

In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product, $\boldsymbol{q}_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_2=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,-1)^{\top}$ form an orthonormal basis. A vector $\boldsymbol{x}$ has coordinates $y_1=\sqrt{2}$ and $y_2=3\sqrt{2}$ in this basis. What is $\boldsymbol{x}$ in standard coordinates?

Let $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$ be orthonormal in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, and suppose $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{q}_i=0$ for every $i=1,\ldots,k$. What can be concluded about $\boldsymbol{x}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$ for every $k$, since an orthonormal set is linearly independent
$\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$ if $k=n$; for $k<n$, any $\boldsymbol{x}$ orthogonal to their span

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}^2$ use the inner product $\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=2x_1y_1+x_2y_2$ instead of the dot product. Which statement about the standard basis $\boldsymbol{e}_1=(1,0)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{e}_2=(0,1)^{\top}$ is correct for this inner product?
options: It is orthogonal but not orthonormal, since $\langle\boldsymbol{e}_1,\boldsymbol{e}_1\rangle=2$
It is orthonormal, since the standard basis is orthonormal for every inner product
It is neither orthogonal nor normalised, since $\langle\boldsymbol{e}_1,\boldsymbol{e}_2\rangle\neq0$
It is normalised but not orthogonal, since the weight $2$ tilts the axes

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, $\boldsymbol{q}_1=\tfrac{1}{3}(1,2,2)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_2=\tfrac{1}{3}(2,1,-2)^{\top}$ form an orthonormal basis of a plane $W$. What is the distance $\|\boldsymbol{b}-\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}\|$ from $\boldsymbol{b}=(9,0,0)^{\top}$ to $W$?

In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ and norm $\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}$, for which vectors $(a,b)^{\top}$ is $\tfrac{1}{5}(3,4)^{\top},(a,b)^{\top}$ an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
